stories.headline: Iraq Orders Army Into Kataib Hezbollah Stronghold Amid Oil Smuggling Probe
stories.summary:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the armed forces to move into Jurf al-Nasr, a town south of Baghdad that serves as a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group. Government spokesman Haidar al-Aboudi announced the order on Monday through the state-run Iraqi News Agency. A senior Iraqi official told Al Jazeera Arabic that the group has until Friday to leave the area.

The move follows a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centered on the town, which is alleged to harbor illicit oil refineries. An investigative committee reported what it called clear tampering with pipelines passing through the area, along with attempts to conceal the traces. Sources told Reuters the smuggling has cost the government hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021. The probe has led to the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials, and security agencies have been told to stop tankers carrying oil products from leaving the area.

Kataib Hezbollah denied the allegations, saying an inspection found no interference with pipelines. It described the campaign as blackmail aimed at forcing it to give up its weapons. The deployment comes amid pressure from the United States and some Gulf states on Baghdad to curb Tehran's influence, and while Iran and the US are engaged in open hostilities. Analysts say the oil probe is a calculated effort to cut off the finances of armed factions that refuse to integrate into the state, and the order raises the prospect of direct confrontation between government troops and the group.

stories.headline: Five EU Countries Announce Migrant Deportation Hub in Rwanda
stories.summary:
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands announced they will open a migrant "return hub" in Rwanda in 2027 as part of a broader push to increase deportations. The announcement came at a joint press conference in Vienna, where Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the aim is to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers organizing deadly Mediterranean crossings.

The scheme will apply to migrants who have exhausted their legal avenues to remain in the five countries. The Dutch government said the first phase will return only single men, with the Netherlands focusing on people from countries in Rwanda's region. Deportees may integrate into Rwandan society, with rights to residence, education, healthcare and work, or return to their home countries. Diplomatic sources told AFP the hub will begin as a pilot of about 100 people, with roughly 20 from each country. The International Organization for Migration may play an ancillary role.

The plan follows a recent EU reform permitting hubs outside the bloc. The governments say it complies with EU and international law, while human rights bodies warn it could violate migrants' rights. It differs from the scrapped British plan, which would have sent people to Rwanda to have claims processed and was abandoned in 2024 after legal challenges. Downing Street has not ruled out joining and says it will watch with interest. Rwanda's interior minister, Vincent Biruta, called it a safe, legal and dignified solution.

stories.headline: Burnham to Declare Brexit 'Has Not Worked,' Pledges New EU Deal
stories.summary:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to say Brexit "has not worked" and that he will sign a new agreement with the European Union. He will speak at the Lord Mayor's banquet in the City of London on Monday, ahead of a summit this week with European leaders. He says the agreements could raise GDP by 0.4 percent, about 17 billion pounds, covering food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

Burnham is expected to say the promise to take back control was not delivered and left a needlessly hard Brexit that harmed business. He will say he would sign a deal if it fits Labour's manifesto and red lines, improves the Brexit settlement, and delivers tangible improvements in everyday life. He told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK had lost more than it gained.

EU relations minister Hamish Falconer said Britain could have a voice in the room but no vote on EU food policy. He said the deal could include an exit clause, since Brussels is worried a future Reform or Conservative government could undo it. Former prime minister Boris Johnson said Britain would absolutely vote for Brexit again and warned that making the issue a priority would damage Burnham and his party.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Declines Maryland Gun-Carry Challenge and California Bias-Training Case
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear a broad challenge to Maryland's restrictions on carrying firearms in many public places, including parks and public transportation. The refusal leaves in place state laws barring guns in widely used public spaces, a point gun-rights advocates have contested since the court expanded Second Amendment protections in recent years.

The court also declined to take up a challenge to California's mandatory implicit bias training for medical license renewals. Justice Clarence Thomas led a firm dissent, arguing the court should have reviewed the free-speech concerns involved. Critics of such programs describe them as diversity, equity and inclusion training that compels speech, while supporters say they address disparities in medical care.

Declining review sets no nationwide precedent, but it lets the lower-court rulings stand. The decisions follow the court's recent agreement to hear a challenge to the administration's suspension of asylum access at the southern border.

stories.headline: Update: Musk and Tech Allies Back 'Bring Jensen Back' Campaign to Reinstate Ex-Nvidia Chief
stories.summary:
Allies of Jensen Huang are lobbying Nvidia's board to reinstate him as chief executive, days after he resigned over a scandal involving two extramarital affairs. One relationship was with Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying for China, and the other was allegedly with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. An open letter on a website called "Stand with Jensen" has gathered more than 175,000 signatures, including those of SpaceX's Elon Musk and Epic Games chief Tim Sweeney.

The letter urges the board to "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts," unless it can show compelling evidence that his removal serves the company's interests. Signers say they are concerned he was removed "without meaningful due process." Musk has claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost without Huang. The Financial Times reported that Huang is discussing a possible return with confidants and that a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives is being assembled, including an effort to win White House support. A representative for Huang declined to comment, and the BBC understands reinstatement is unlikely while Nvidia's internal investigation continues.

The affair has also raised national security questions. It has created tensions between the Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Megaspeed, Alice Huang's former firm, and whether the chips reached China despite US export restrictions. Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the relationship. Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China.

The case has drawn criticism from Republicans, including some in the MAGA base, while supporters of Huang argue the company risks losing its leader of the AI boom without a full factual record. Nvidia is among the world's most valuable companies and a central player in AI expansion, so the outcome matters for markets and for US-China technology policy.

stories.headline: Two Mass Shootings in South Africa Leave 17 Dead
stories.summary:
South African police are investigating the killings of 17 people in two unrelated shootings on Sunday night. Eight men were shot dead in a minibus outside Pietermaritzburg in KwaZulu-Natal province, where police found a white seven-seater vehicle riddled with bullet holes. Hours later, nine people, six men and three women, were found shot dead inside a four-room shack in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria.

No motive has been established in either case. Police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said investigators are collecting evidence to determine the motive and the identity of the suspects, and a manhunt is under way. In Gauteng, the provincial commissioner has mobilised crime intelligence and tracking teams. Residents said they initially mistook the gunshots for thunder and lightning.

The shootings add to a run of mass killings in the country. In September, 28 people died in two separate attacks, including 18 killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar near Johannesburg. Much of the violence has been linked to turf wars between gangs involved in drug trafficking and illegal mining, and illegal firearms are widespread.

President Cyril Ramaphosa described organised crime in February as "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development." The military has been deployed alongside police in five high-murder provinces, including Gauteng. Police recorded 5,427 murders between April and June 2026, about 60 a day, a 6 percent decline.

stories.headline: Treasury Secretary Bessent Moves to Military Base Amid Iranian Assassination Threat
stories.summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and his family have relocated to a military base after reported Iranian threats against him, becoming the latest senior Trump administration official to live behind military gates. A source familiar with the situation told Fox News Digital that security concerns rose after The Wall Street Journal published an online photo that allowed his Georgetown home to be geolocated. The source said the news media "has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials."

A senior administration official said earlier that threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage," without elaborating. Attorney General Todd Blanche reportedly moved to a military base around March. The reports come amid the ongoing US-Israel war with Iran and a history of alleged Tehran-backed plots, including a 2022 Justice Department charge against an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps member in a murder-for-hire plot targeting John Bolton, and a 2024 disclosure that an Iranian operative was tasked with planning an assassination of Trump.

Former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino said protection decisions are driven by threat assessments, and he blamed a "permission structure on the left for violence" combined with the ability to track officials online for a surge in threats. Critics of the administration have generally argued that officials should be held to scrutiny and that reporting on public figures is legitimate, though the pool coverage focused on the administration's account. Fox also cited a US intelligence memo warning that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target Americans abroad.

stories.headline: Mayor Mamdani Disbands NYPD Strategic Response Group
stories.summary:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democrat, announced Monday that the city has disbanded the NYPD's Strategic Response Group, the department's counterterrorism and protest-response unit. In a joint statement with Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, he said the move will "transform" how city officials approach public safety. He also announced a new community safety division.

The unit has faced criticism for years from civil rights groups that accused it of using excessive force and unduly aggressive tactics against protesters. Mamdani said the decision stemmed from a campaign pledge to disband the group, which he announced in a video released Monday morning.

Supporters of the move say it fulfills a mandate from voters and addresses documented complaints about protest policing. Critics of such steps, often on the right and among police advocates, have argued that specialized units are needed for counterterrorism and large-scale public order operations in a city that is a frequent target. Tisch's joint role in the announcement signals that the department's leadership agreed to the change, though details of how the unit's counterterrorism functions will be reassigned were not provided in the available reporting.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Strikes Bahrain Again as Third US Carrier Group Arrives in Middle East
stories.summary:
Iran carried out a six-drone attack on a US airbase in Bahrain early Sunday, the second strike on the Gulf state in three days. Bahrain said it intercepted "several aerial attacks" before they hit their targets. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the US air defense radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base was targeted, while Bahraini authorities disputed any successful hit. Bahrain had not been targeted since September.

A US official told ABC News that a third aircraft carrier strike group has arrived in the Middle East, with the USS Theodore Roosevelt joining two other carriers in the US Central Command area. President Trump shared a message saying "May God protect our troops." The attacks follow minor US strikes on Iran's Qeshm island in recent weeks, and the US and Iran remain locked in a standoff over the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has reiterated that a path to ending the conflict with the US remains open.

The war began in February, when Trump announced major combat operations against Iran. Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken warned on Sunday that a US ground invasion of Iran would be an "absolute disaster." The Justice Department also charged three men with ties to the IRGC over roughly 18 planned attacks in Europe, including a thwarted plot against a UK airbase housing US personnel and aircraft.

The BBC reported that Democrats' midterm victory could lead to a more critical approach to the war in the next Congress. Republicans have generally backed the military campaign as necessary to counter Iran, while many Democrats are pressing for congressional oversight and a path to ending the conflict.

stories.headline: Update: Senate Democratic Leadership Fight Opens as Van Hollen Challenges Schumer
stories.summary:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland appeared on CNN, ABC and Fox News on Sunday to escalate his bid to lead the incoming Senate Democratic majority in place of Chuck Schumer. He said he has a "wide-open" path to victory. Democrats clinched the Senate in the midterms after winning the House, taking several states Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

The Hill reported Saturday that Schumer's allies expect him to win more than 40 votes in the leadership contest. Van Hollen called that report "a bunch of nonsense" and said several senators claimed by Schumer's team have privately pledged to back him. Sen.-elect Scott Colom of Mississippi, who flipped a seat blue for the first time in decades, urged Democrats on NBC to invest more in Southern states.

On the Republican side, Senate Republicans kept John Thune as leader by acclamation after a heated closed-door meeting. A Politico poll shows tension within the party over its direction after its worst midterm performance in a generation, and some Republicans say rising stars should skip 2028.

Democrats are weighing an agenda that includes Medicaid restoration, ACA tax credit expansion and housing aid. Axios notes that to secure policy wins quickly, they may need to work with Trump. Meanwhile, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche and Texas US Attorney Aaron Reitz criticized Democrats, including Sen. Elizabeth Warren, over plans for investigations of Trump and his allies, with Reitz demanding she preserve documents. Democrats describe such oversight as a core congressional duty.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Asks Congress to Fund New Air Traffic Control System After Nationwide Ground Stop
stories.summary:
President Trump on Sunday asked Congress to fund a new air traffic control system following Friday's nationwide ground stop of all US flights, the longest in 25 years. "If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently," he wrote. He said it would be "the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World."

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy appeared on four Sunday shows and blamed the lack of congressional funding. He earlier said overloaded routers tied to maintenance work by contractor L3Harris triggered the stop. Officials also cited aging infrastructure and legacy technology, and Duffy said the precise cause was not yet fully known.

The disruption continued Sunday, with about 2,000 canceled flights and more than 8,000 delays. Even NFL crews were affected, with four officials working two games. United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby called the episode a "call to action" to modernize the system, saying he has spoken with both parties.

Republicans point to years of underinvestment and Congress's funding role, while Democrats and some critics, including former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, have taken aim at the administration's handling. The funding request is likely to become an early test of how Trump and the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress can cooperate.

stories.headline: Nearly 2,200 Migrants Reach Canary Islands in Two Days as Spain Declares Emergency
stories.summary:
Nearly 2,200 migrants reached Spain's Canary Islands by boat over the past two days, Spain's maritime rescue service said Sunday. The service assisted 1,324 people aboard 14 dinghies, most of whom landed on El Hierro, an island of about 12,000 residents. That figure approached the route's daily rescue record of 1,461, set on Nov. 7, 2020.

Spain declared a migration emergency on the islands on Tuesday after a rise in arrivals, particularly from sub-Saharan Africa. More than 13,000 of the just over 28,000 people who reached Spain by sea from January through October landed in the Canaries, according to the Interior Ministry. Red Cross staff provided dry clothes, food and water at the port.

The Atlantic route is among the world's deadliest, with most boats leaving from Mauritania. The surge comes as Spain prepares for an early general election in two weeks, which is likely to keep immigration at the center of political debate. In July, tens of thousands crossed from Morocco into Ceuta in two days, and up to 15,000 remained.
